subtopic: FURTHER ANNOUNCEMENT ON VISIT OF UNITED KINGDOM PRIME MINISTER

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FURTHER ANNOUNCEMENT ON VISIT OF UNITED KINGDOM PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 17 the Prime Minister announced that Right Hon. Harold Macmillan, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, accompanied by Lady Dorothy, would be paying a brief visit to Ottawa on April 7 and 8. Hon. members will have heard with great pleasure on today's news broadcast that the visit is now to be of longer duration. As a result of talks which Mr. Diefenbaker had yesterday in London, the dates of the visit are now arranged for April 8 to April 12.
Mr. Macmillan and Lady Dorothy will be the guests of Their Excellencies the Governor General and Madame Vanier during their stay in Ottawa. As they are arriving here on a Saturday it is planned that they shall spend a quiet week end, which will then be followed by two days of talks with ministers on questions of mutual concern.
The United Kingdom Prime Minister will be arriving in Ottawa from Washington, where he will just have completed talks with President Kennedy. As the right hon. Prime Minister said in the house on February 16 when he first expressed the hope that Mr. Macmillan might visit Canada, it has become a welcome custom that whenever the United Kingdom Prime Minister has visited the president of the United States for consultations, he has almost invariably visited Canada either before or after. Such visits are not only useful but give us a great deal of pleasure, and I am sure all members of the house will welcome the news that Right Hon. Mr. Macmillan and Lady Dorothy have found it possible to spend a few days with us here in Ottawa.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FURTHER ANNOUNCEMENT ON VISIT OF UNITED KINGDOM PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house will have welcomed the statement made by the Acting Prime Minister. I know that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and his wife will receive the warm welcome which is traditionally accorded prime ministers of the United Kingdom, and I hope their stay in Canada will be both useful and pleasant.

subtopic: FURTHER ANNOUNCEMENT ON VISIT OF UNITED KINGDOM PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the visit of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom is to be of longer duration, and since parliament will be in session for part of that time, I would hope that it might be possible for the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, as I suggested earlier, to address a joint session of both houses of parliament.
I would think these talks could be very useful, particularly on the return of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from the United States. As we all so well know, there are many urgent outstanding world problems that require the attention of the leaders of the world. I am certain that discussions between our own Prime Minister and Prime Minister Macmillan regarding trade questions and questions involving the peace of the world would be particularly useful following his discussions with President Kennedy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the house will bear with me with regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia to the effect that Mr. Macmillan should be asked to address the members of the Senate and House of Commons. I am not yet in a position to announce whether that will be possible, but I am hoping it will be.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF REGULATIONS RESPECTING ACCELERATED DEPRECIATION OF ASSETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that the regulations providing for special capital cost allowances have been printed and are being distributed today to members of both houses and other interested parties. These regulations provide that accelerated depreciation may be claimed in respect of most types of assets acquired after December 31, 1960, if the assets are used in making a product not previously produced in Canada or in a surplus manpower area. Such assets are eligible for double depreciation for one year on the basis of the capital expenditure incurred for such equipment. The extra allowance can be applied in any of the first three years after the asset is acquired.
Companies acquiring assets which they believe may be eligible for special capital cost allowances should communicate with the depreciation certification branch, Department of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa. Copies of

Labour Conditions
an explanatory memorandum, the regulations and application forms will be sent to them. This material is available in French and English.
Municipal or area authorities wishing to have their localities or areas designated as surplus manpower areas should communicate with the Department of Labour, which will be responsible for receiving and studying such applications.

I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that until such time as we have given further study to the announcement made by the minister, the fact that he has made this announcement only indicates the confusion and uncertainty on the government benches.

REPORT ON CONFERENCE TO EXPEDITE MOVEMENT THROUGH PACIFIC COAST PORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the house an interim report on the conference held in Vancouver on Monday and Tuesday and continuing today with regard to expediting the movement of grain through west coast ports. There were some 40 senior officers representing 18 different organizations in attendance, and it is my belief that this was a perfect example of a productivity council in action. The grain gathering companies from the prairies, the two great railway companies, the two labour unions affected, the merchants exchange, the grain exchange and the government agencies concerned pooled their information, and as a result I believe I am able to say now that there will be an increase ranging from 15 to 25 per cent in the movement of grain out of these ports in the next few months.
I was asked at the meeting to correct an erroneous statement by the hon. member for Vancouver East which appears in Hansard for last Wednesday, the day I announced the conference. At that time he said, as found on page 2593 of Hansard:
It is many, many years since there have been any extensions to the port of Vancouver. As a matter of fact, the facilities of the port are less now than they were as a result of a fire many years ago. The facilities lost then have never been replaced.
I simply want to say at this time that when I was in Vancouver I was given enough information by people there who are very proud of their port to indicate that this statement was wrong, and I will give the hon. member all the statistics I have to that effect. I simply want to say that there have been many facilities added to the port in the last few years, including storage for grain 90205-6-176
Grain Shipments
to the extent of an additional capacity of three or four million bushels.
Finally, may I say that I think the conference will result in a permanent body being set up for liaison and the co-ordination of the movement of grain through the western ports. A permanent body will also be set up, I hope, to handle public relations that involve several organizations.

maintopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE TO EXPEDITE MOVEMENT THROUGH PACIFIC COAST PORTS
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, the person making the recommendations to the conference was the Minister of Agriculture. I asked the representatives of these 18 organizations to see what they could do about speeding up the movement of grain through west coast ports in view of the market situation. I suggested several things to them and they promised their co-operation. The meeting broke up into committees yesterday afternoon and those committees are continuing to meet today and possibly tomorrow. I will not know until the meetings have been completed just what final steps will be taken. However, from what I heard yesterday I believe I can assure the house that the suggestion I made of an increase of 15 per cent to 25 per cent in shipments through the port will be realized.

maintopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE TO EXPEDITE MOVEMENT THROUGH PACIFIC COAST PORTS
speechtext:
In answer to that question I may say that the handling of grain through any port is a very complicated

Grain Shipments
business. Before the conference I was under the impression that there was a lack of coordination in the handling of this movement as among these 18 organizations, but I think the conference established that these things can be ameliorated.
In so far as the tie-up of ships a week or 10 days ago is concerned, I think that can be explained to some degree by the fact that a number of ships arrived at once. As an illustration of this point, may I say that today we expected five ships to enter the harbour. They did not come because of storms on the Pacific. They are expected in today or tomorrow, but there are three berths lying idle today. We are not loading to maximum capacity. These things cannot be prevented by any amount of planning. What we are trying to do is to set up a permanent liaison group which will funnel information to all the groups concerned so there will be no tie-up for which we can be held responsible for lack of planning.

speechtext: Will the minister comment on statements made in Vancouver that the government, not the board, made the sale to the Chinese, and the government failed to advise the board about these special requirements?

maintopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE TO EXPEDITE MOVEMENT THROUGH PACIFIC COAST PORTS
speechtext:
I do not think the press reports are altogether accurate. We made the announcement publicly in the house, which would be the first official warning they would have of the sale. The responsibility in the next stage would be that of the agents hired by the Chinese resources company to make known when these ships were going to arrive. A responsibility then would devolve upon the Canadian wheat board to berth these ships at the various berths where the grades required were available. Of course it is the responsibility of the board to get these grades into the port ahead of time.
I believe that as a result of suddenly moving the port up to capacity a number of things happened about which we have heard. I cannot guarantee that there will not be more of these tie-ups. It is my judgment that there will be more than we have had in the past, because we are trying to use the facilities to maximum capacity and when you do that there are bound to be these tie-ups.

January 18, 1961-Telegram to the Prime Minister from Mr. Angus Keiller, president, Lodge No. 456, I.A. of M., c/o Fairey Aviation Company of Canada Limited, Patricia Bay airport, B.C.
"It is come to our attention that twelve Neptune aircraft based at Comox BC will be flown out of the province for painting at Victoria airport Fairey Aviation has all the men and facilities for carrying out this work as you are aware the unemployment situation in the Victoria district is acute and if Fairey Aviation were forced to close due to lack of military work it would be disastrous as most of our members are employed by Fairey Aviation the only aircraft overhaul plant on Vancouver Island would you sir on our behalf intervene to divert at least some of this work to Fairey Aviation trusting this meets with your favourable consideration."
January 26, 1961-Telegraphic reply from the secretary to the Prime Minister to Mr. Keiller*
"With reference to your telegram of January 18 I would advise you that the awarding of the contract for the painting of eleven Neptunes based at Comox was decided as the result of competitive tenders and the lowest tenderer is being awarded the contract stop all firms in the western area who are considered to be in a position to complete this work satisfactorily were invited to tender and in each case the firms were suffering from serious cut-backs in employment stop the competitive tender is the normal way for the Department of Defence Production to do business stop I can assure you however that with respect to any other work that may arise which Fairey Aviation at Patricia Bay are capable of carrying out this company will be invited to tender under the normal practice stop"

Toone, secretary treasurer, Victoria labour
council to Hon. Raymond O'Hurley:
"This council has in the past requested the allocation of work on behalf of the Department of National Defence to the plant of Fairey Aviation Company of Canada Limited, Sidney, B.C. may we again urge that consideration be given to this.
We are given to understand that painting, servicing and overhauling of aircraft of the Department of National Defence in this area is sent out of this province to be done, when the facilities for such work are available at the Sidney plant within a very short distance of the aircraft base.
Over the years, this plant has obtained the required tools and experienced personnel to deal with such work, without which both the industry and the jobs will be lost to this area, with the resulting increase in unemployment.
In view of the overall economy, we believe that this industry should be encouraged on Vancouver Island, and every effort made to maintain the craftsman in employment.
We therefore trust that favourable consideration will be given to the allocation of work to this plant; and we look forward to your assurance in this regard."
February 6, 1961-Reply letter from Hon.
Raymond O'Hurley to Mr. Toone-
"I have your letter dated January 18, 1961, in which you request that consideration be given to the allocation of defence work to the plant of the Fairey Aviation Company of Canada Limited, Sidney, B.C. You refer specifically to a recent requirement for the painting of eleven Neptune aircraft which, as a result of competitive tender, was allocated out of your area.
In reply I would state that as this requirement had never previously been carried out by any of our western contractors it was decided by my department that the requirement should be thrown open to competition. An additional consideration leading to this decision was the progressive decline in workload, with resultant lay-offs, at all plants west of and including Winnipeg. My department was of the opinion that a competitive tender would serve a dual purpose, in that it not only would result in the utmost in economies, but would also bolster the morale of the contractors concerned by affording them an opportunity to gain additional work on their own merits. The Fairey Aviation Company of Canada Limited was one of three companies invited to tender, but quoted a figure considerably higher than the lowest tenderer, who was ultimately selected to perform the work.

We concur in your general comments concerning the overall economy of the area, and in particular to the need for ensuring that the Fairey Aviation Company of Canada Limited be given every opportunity to compete for such work as they are qualified and equipped to perform. You have my assurance that these considerations will always be borne in mind by my department when dealing with future requirements in your area."

speechtext:
I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the form of this question, which reads:
In the tax-sharing arrangement provided in the legislation of 1956 and accepted by the government of Quebec, is there any limitation on the constitutional right of that province to levy and collect any tax it would have the right to levy under the constitution?
I presume that by his reference to the legislation of 1956 the hon. member means the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, but you will note, Mr. Speaker, the statement that "the arrangement provided in the legislation" was accepted by the government in Quebec. I am not aware of any arrangement accepted or any agreement entered into by the government of Quebec in pursuance of that legislation. On the contrary, the province of Quebec did not enter into any tax rental or collection agreement under or in pursuance of the terms of that particular statute.

I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman read the question correctly, then substituted a word which is not in the question. He substituted the word "agreement", which has nothing to do with the question whatsoever, for the word "arrangement". The hon. gentleman is perfectly well aware that the government of the province of Quebec did accept that arrangement and has been receiving equalization payments, and I suggest it would be desirable if, instead of misrepresenting the question, the hon. gentleman would answer it.

Mr. Speaker, the bill sets out in some detail the provisions that were forecast in the resolution. The tariff board will be given the power to sit as two panels simultaneously, and there is a provision allowing the chairman to direct that any inquiries under section 4 may be made by any member or members of the board designated by him. It appears obvious, therefore, that when the measure is passed and becomes law the board, both in dealing with appeals and in making certain inquiries, will be in a position to do a much larger amount of work. We still feel that this bill cannot be separated from the other changes that are being made in the customs tariff having to do with the definition of goods of a class or kind, and that the insertion of the word "approximately" will mean that the tariff board will have a host of applications to deal with that it would not otherwise have. This seems a part of the government program, to change the rules on tariffs in such a way as to provide higher tariffs for a much larger range of goods. This underlines something we have suspected for a long time; that the present government is following an old traditional Tory policy in providing a higher level of tariffs.
When the measure was being discussed in committee certain questions were asked of the minister and I hope that he will give the house the information that was asked for at that time. He was asked how many applications before the board have to do with the question of class or kind and I hope that he will inform the house as to the statistics in this regard. Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Welland asked how many of the 69 appeals now pending before the tariff board concern cases where the class or kind definition is involved. I am informed on inquiry that there are 17 such cases and three other cases where this question may possibly be involved either directly or indirectly.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked for a tabulation as to the eight references pending before the board. They are as follows, Mr. Chairman:	No. 120 is the
chemicals reference. The hearings on this important and very comprehensive reference began in 1960 and will probably continue throughout 1961 and perhaps beyond. The second is No. 123, the radio, television and electronics reference. No. 125 is the textiles reference: there have been several reports received from the tariff board in this regard but the reference is not complete as yet so far as reports are concerned.
The next is No. 127, in relation to nails. The hearings on this reference have been held but the report has not yet been submitted. The next is No. 128, a reference concerning engineers' and architects' plans, drawings and blueprints. The hearings in regard to this reference were held last month, but of course the report has not yet been received. No. 129 is the reference on tableware and glassware for decorating. The hearings on this reference are scheduled to commence on March 20.
The next is No. 130, a reference concerning machinery and equipment for use in the mining industry and the oil and gas industries. The hearings on this reference have been scheduled for May, June and September next. The next is No. 131, a reference respecting oilseeds, vegetable oils and related products. The hearings have not yet been held in this regard. Obviously the plans in relation to the scheduling of these remaining references will depend of course on the passage of the present bill and the ability of the tariff board then to commence sitting in two panels.

The house resumed from Tuesday, March 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for the second reading of Bill No. C-71, respecting the civil service of Canada.

This legislation, designed to improve the Civil Service Act, is most important because more than ever before a good civil service is absolutely essential to good government. The need for properly qualified civil servants can be attributed primarily to the increasing role of government with the result that we have to rely more and more on a number of experts, highly qualified administrators. Their position and prestige should be consistent with their new importance. The complex issues which government has to face require the advice of highly qualified people, although ministers must always take responsibility for public administration decisions on policy matters.
In parallel development our Canadian universities and other institutions have been producing for several decades an increasing number of experts in the social sciences and in various fields of government activity with the result that while the need for expert advice was growing rapidly in the government service, the number of Canadians highly qualified to meet that need was also increasing.
It is widely recognized that the Canadian civil service is one of the best in the world. It is composed at all levels of men and women who are well qualified to perform their important functions, who are devoted to the service of their country and entirely loyal to the government of the day; and those who give loyalty and service have a right to expect confidence, support and encouragement, conditions that will make them more effective.
The quality of our civil service is also due to our legislation which has been based since 1918 on the merit principle. The adherence to that principle has enabled the Canadian government to attract to the service highly qualified people in various fields who have decided to make a career in the public service and who very often refused better paid careers outside it.

Civil Service Act
Although the Civil Service Act has proved to be of great value to the civil servants and to the government over the years and has provided a general framework which has led to good relations between the government and its employees, experience has shown that the legislation enacted in 1918 needed to be changed in several respects in the light of the important changes in the role of government which have occurred in Canada since the end of world war II. As a matter of fact, there have been practically no changes since 1918. That is why at the beginning of 1957 the then prime minister, Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, asked the members of the civil service commission to review the act and the regulations and to examine the role of the commission in the machinery of government and to prepare a report including recommendations as to desirable changes to be made to our legislation.
It is a cause for uneasiness that so many top officials have left the public service in order to teach in universities or to work in industry or other professions. Whatever the reasons given to explain those resignations, they faced us with a disquieting situation; highly qualified personnel are leaving, and as a result serious damage is being done to the efficiency of public administration.
One cause of uneasiness has been the delay of the government in introducing legislation following the publication of the Heeney report. That report was presented to the government in December, 1958. Its recommendations were detailed and concrete, and legislation should have been introduced in 1959 for final consideration during the 1960 session. However, the government has delayed the introduction of its legislation until March 1961.
Another source of concern is the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), not the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion), is the government spokesman on matters related to the civil service and is introducing this bill. As we all know the Secretary of State has always been responsible to parliament for those matters. The fact that the Minister of Finance has become the champion and the defender of the civil service, after his performance on the salary issue last year, is a surprise to us and I am sure it is a source of concern for all government employees. At some stage during this debate I hope the minister will explain why he and not the Secretary of State is introducing this legislation.
We on this side of the house want to express our gratitude to Mr. Heeney and his two colleagues Miss Addison and Mr. Pelletier, for the most valuable report they have prepared on the subject of this legislation. We

believe that their report will provide a most useful basis for the discussion and appraisal of the government legislation which is now before us.
The Heeney report contains recommendations regarding all aspects of the civil service including its relations with the government. I am sure that all of us in this house will agree with most, if not all, of the eight objectives set out in the report as the basis for this new legislation. The commission has made specific recommendations regarding organization and classification, compensation and allowances, recruitment, selection, appointment and promotion, transfers, discipline, appeals, the veteran's preference, languages, qualifications, and exemptions from the Civil Service Act, et cetera. That is all very well.
While we will want to discuss all the provisions of the bill, we intend to put special emphasis on the definition and the clarification of the rights of civil servants. I well recall that in a speech made before the institute of public administration of Canada in 1959, a member of the commission, Mr. Paul Pelletier, has this to say on this matter:
-Since 1918, federal civil servants have had no legal rights whatever, except two. The first is referred to in section 45 of the Civil Service Act which provides that civil servants shall, on a mandatory basis, be granted certain statutory holidays. The second was only granted in May, 1953, with the enactment of the Public Service Superannuation Act-and that is the civil servant's contractual entitlement to pension under certain conditions. But otherwise, the civil servant has no statutory rights. He is not entitled to his pay cheque until it is in his pocket. He can legally be dismissed without cause and without notice. X would not wish to suggest for one moment that civil servants are dismissed frivolously. Quite the contrary. Nor would I suggest that any civil servant is in any kind of danger of not receiving his fortnightly pay cheque at the appropriate time. But the fact remains that his statutory rights are virtually non-existent. The commission felt that at the present state of our constitutional development civil servants should be given certain statutory rights.
We on this side of the house completely agree with that statement. We also feel that in this respect the bill does not go far enough, and at a later stage of the discussion we shall make specific proposals to the government regarding a fuller recognition of these statutory rights of civil servants.
I do not intend at this stage to discuss all the provisions of the bill. We intend to postpone this detailed consideration until the proposed legislation has been considered by the special committee. For the time being, I wish to confine my remarks to one issue only-an issue which I consider to be basic-

namely, the question of collective bargaining, or, as I would prefer to call it, collective negotiation.
The lack of statutory rights is well illustrated by the way in which salaries in the civil service are determined. In 1959 the civil service commission decided to reconsider the salary question. After consultation with the staff associations and with the assistance of its pay research bureau the commission recommended to the Minister of Finance that a general increase in salaries be granted. After long delays, the minister announced in October that he could not accept the commission's recommendation. No adequate reason was given by the minister in justification of his stand. The report of the commission was not released, with the result that civil servants could not even know what increases in salary had been recommended by the commission and refused by the Minister of Finance.
Such a situation is intolerable in Canada and must be remedied. But the present bill does not provide any adequate improvement in this respect. I shall not refer in detail to clause 7, though the minister did refer to it last night, except to say that consultation is possible and can be initiated by the staff or by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

If the minister does not object, I will read the clause:
The commission and such members of the public service as the Minister of Finance may designate shall from time to time consult with representatives of appropriate organizations and associations of employees with respect to pay and other terms and conditions of employment at the request of such representatives or whenever in the opinion of the commission or the Minister of Finance, as the case may be, such consultation is necessary or desirable in the interests of the civil service or the government.
This is not satisfactory. Even if under this new provision the staff associations were to be placed in a position to initiate consultations this new prerogative will be ineffectual. Consultations will never be a substitute for genuine negotiations. How are the civil servants to know that the government had adopted a course which requires consultation? The time has come to face the issue of collective bargaining squarely and frankly. In our country all municipal employees, including policemen and firemen, have obtained the right to collective bargaining. In the federal field the majority of the employees of crown corporations already enjoy such a right. But ordinary civil servants have no right whatsoever in this respect. This has become a serious anomaly and an unfair discrimination.

Procedure at the hearing is not overly formal. Each side has one spokesman who is assisted by a group of advisers. The spokesman for the claimant is first in reading his statement of the case. This is substantially what was submitted to the tribunal in advance except that in reading it there is an opportunity to amplify some points and amend any errors or inconsistencies that might have been overlooked. According to Professor Frankel, more than 600 cases have been brought before the arbitration tribunal since 1925 and all but 25 awards were unanimous.
The Whitley council system, as applied in Great Britain, may not be completely suitable to Canadian conditions. This experience of 30 years shows, however, that the right to genuine negotiations and arbitration in the civil service is compatible with our system of parliamentary democracy and is conducive to good relations between the government and its employees.
The views of the official opposition on this most important issue can be summarized as follows:
1.	We believe that the present Canadian system which provides only for consultations is completely inadequate to protect the fundamental right of the civil service for participation in collective negotiations, while our view is that the right to strike should not be granted to the civil service and that a strike should not be tolerated in the government service.
2.	We believe that civil servants should be granted the right to joint negotiations and arbitration provided that the supremacy of the parliament is safeguarded.
3.	We do not intend at this stage to put forward a concrete and detailed proposal which would embody those rights but we will suggest such a system, if necessary, when we reach the committee stage.
4.	We firmly believe that this most important issue should be considered objectively and carefully by all hon. members of this house and that it should not become the subject of a partisan controversy.
The bill is one of the most important that can be submitted to any parliament because its purpose is to provide for the efficiency and the integrity of the civil service which is so essential to modern democracy. I want

at this stage to quote the conclusions of Professor E. N. Gladden's book entitled "Civil Service or Bureaucracy".
The nation needs more than ever before a civil service capable of the highest devotion and sacrifice to its service and this presupposes an esteem, on the part of those who serve, much higher than exists today. We need a body of civil servants even more efficient than those of a past age and this presupposes professional standards far above anything visualized before. The officials of the future will need higher qualifications to deal with much more difficult tasks and situations. They will need to combine a sense of political impartiality as high as ever with an awareness of the world only achievable through the maintenance of a living interest in all that goes on in life in the broadest sense.
Such ends can no longer be achieved through a narrow oligarchic system admirably suited to a Platonic world. In the new civil service there will have to be embodied the principle of equal opportunity toward which the wider community is gradually moving. The community will not get its new civil service on the cheap, but from its efficiency it will derive an economy that mediocrity will never produce. Bureaucracy, whether of the efficient or the inefficient variety, will be dear at any price, as all history shows. Above all the new civil service, like the new world, will only emerge on the wings of a more liberal understanding.
Mr. Speaker, we intend to study the bill very carefully and see to it that the best possible legislation is approved by parliament. We owe it to the civil service to do so and in so doing we feel that we will render as well a great service to all Canadians who have been throughout the years so ably and faithfully served by a civil service second to none in any parliamentary democracy. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are indeed pleased to again have this bill before parliament and to note with interest some of the comments that were made by the minister. We are aware of the fact that the civil service in Canada has been built up from a very small beginning some years ago to a necessarily large but efficient force and that any change in the Civil Service Act must be studied carefully.

I am sure we are all aware that the civil service has done a service to Canada, and will continue to do so, but will be able to operate only in as effective a manner as is allowed under the legislation. I believe that we will find many faults in the suggested proposals and the operation of the act as it will be enforced because over the years the situation has changed very dramatically. I believe the foremost thought in the minds of parliamentarians at the time the Civil Service Act was last amended in 1919 related to the providing of a protection against political patronage. In spite of this government and previous governments the question of political patronage has not been a threat to the effective operation of the civil service that it was many years ago.
We are now faced with a changed time and a changing situation which might allow patronage to exist in the civil service. Patronage or a tendency to patronage generally exists in large organizations and therefore the necessity is self-evident for a strong grievance procedure, strong protection and strong agreements.
We believe that some change must take place in the operation of the civil service commission itself. It might even be suggested by the civil service commission that if it were to function as the representative of management in relation to wage negotiations and conditions of work, then it would not serve a useful function at all. The government is indicating in the changes it is making that the trend and the tendency may be toward delegating negotiating authority from the civil service commission itself to the departmental heads. I strongly suggest to the minister that this would not be a satisfactory situation. I suggest that in increasing the authority of the departmental heads we are opening the door to patronage in the civil service.
Patronage itself, even in a political sense, is not dead, Mr. Speaker. We all know that the messenger service and some of the other staffs around the House of Commons fall within the purview of patronage, and that you have to talk to a certain member to receive a job even as a messenger. I think these instances are remote and very few in number. I believe that in this respect the civil service has done a remarkable job in remaining beyond the field of political patronage. With this thought in mind, we strongly recommend that the government give a great deal of attention and active consideration in the committee to setting up a much stronger negotiating position and grievance procedure for its employees. If we delegate more authority to the deputy ministers and allow the 90205-6-177J
Civil Service Act
deputy ministers to delegate their authority down through the ranks-which is sure to happen-then difficulties will arise which will be very difficult to solve. In the civil service we should have the same kind of relationship between the employee and the government of Canada as exists in any other type of plant in industry.
We are all aware that the situation in the civil service has been changing in the last number of years. Changes have been taking place which were not contemplated when the act was last amended in 1919. Part of this change has to do with promotions and the opportunities for promotions. When a department or a section of a department, was very small it was quite possible for a junior clerk coming into the department to look into the future and foresee the time when he could be the head of the department, how he could rise in his position and eventually reach the post of deputy minister. We are all aware, I am sure, of the special technical training that is essential to enable a man to fill some of the higher technical positions in the civil service. Because many of these positions are technical in nature it makes promotion difficult within the division.
One of the problems within the civil service, as I have heard it discussed, is the lack of opportunity for promotion of many employees in the lower ranks. When a job within a division is posted or advertised many of the employees are not concerned because they have not the training to fit them for that position. No opportunity is available to permit them to obtain the type of training that would put them in a position to compete with members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or the armed services.
In the armed services we have given, at government expense, training in skills and specific trades to many of the personnel. When a competition is advertised the people who have been trained at government expense can make application for that appointment, and in many instances they will have a better opportunity to get the position than someone lower down the scale in that particular division for the simple reason that opportunities for training are not available to the civil servants, as they are to those in other services who are quite often in direct competition with them.
It has been suggested on many occasions that this type of training be instituted by the departments themselves; that opportunities should be made available to the civil servants to avail themselves of training to fit themselves for job promotion. What happens is that those who are not fitted for promotion at the present time drop whatever desire they may have had for saying that they are white

Civil Service Act
collar workers and therefore are obviously in a preferred position. They now realize that they have a job of which the hours of work, the pay and the fringe benefits are the main features. Therefore they are insisting now, and they are going to increasingly insist in the future more than they did in the past on fair and reasonable terms and a much closer relationship between civil service rates of pay and fringe benefits and those of organized labour.
Unless we are willing to provide the machinery and set up opportunities to permit them to better their own station, and also handle negotiations in a much better way than we have in the last two or three years where hand-outs coming from the government pretty well dribbled down to one section of the civil service and then to another we shall find the civil servants very dissatisfied. These are not the types of negotiations or arrangements that we wish to have or maintain within the civil service.
This matter has been discussed in other countries. I think we should be very proud of the civil service and the job that they have done, particularly when we compare their pay with that received in other countries. New Zealand, Australia, Britain and many other countries have done a great deal more than Canada in establishing a workable type of pattern under which the civil servant feels that he has some rights; that his is not a patronage job; that he cannot be removed because somebody just does not like him; and under which he has grievance procedures which can handle his complaints on a fair and reasonable basis. We in Canada have been lax in this regard, but we have achieved a high degree of satisfaction from our civil service without doing some things that as a government we should have done.
In England in 1923 the Whitley council was established. It is known as the Whitley system. Under this system they have operated with satisfaction in so far as their relations with the government are concerned. Australia and New Zealand have developed similar methods of grievances and contract procedures. I believe that now is an exceptionally good time for the government to examine what has been done in those other countries, and then do something for Canadian civil servants.
One of the reasons that is always advanced as to why we cannot do right by our civil service in relation to grievance procedure and collective bargaining procedure-this has become an important factor-is that many more people are now in the class in which the civil servants felt they were many years ago, that is, they felt they were unique. Recently we

have seen instances of industrial unions trying to organize bank employees, for instance, and to organize employees in the offices of companies where the unions have for many years had a bargaining relationship with respect to the industrial plants of these companies.
When someone says that there should be a grievance procedure, that there should be some direct method of negotiation with the employer, someone will immediately say that if the employees do not get what they want they will go on strike. Although the civil service associations have requested direct negotiation with the employer and the establishment of a grievance procedure, not one of these associations has ever asked for the right to strike if the differences of opinion involved cannot be settled. This right has not been sought and is not contemplated. When people raise the issue that to grant these requests would only result in strike action I think they have not given too much consideration to what has been done in other countries or to what has been done in this country with relation to white collar workers.
I think we should look at what the advantages would be if each employee felt he had the right to negotiate directly with his employer, the right to certain protection under a contract which would not be laid down for him by the civil service commission but which would be a contract in whose negotiation he had some participation and as a result would have some direct interest in the contract under which he was working. I believe the committee will give very serious consideration to the whole matter in relationship not only to what is being done in other countries but also what is being done in respect of employees in other fields of endeavour similar to the civil service of Canada.
Some consideration should be given to the situation as it has developed in some of our provinces. In Saskatchewan, for instance, civil servants have the right to collective bargaining procedures. They have the same right to the benefits of collective bargaining that other employees throughout the province have. This right has not resulted in any serious disruption of the civil service in that province, its relationship with the government of the province or its immunity from political interference.
We are certain that many of these matters will be discussed in the committee. I was pleased that the minister outlined his reasons for introducing the bill last year. I am also pleased that he listened to the representations that were made from many quarters and withheld the bill until there would be an opportunity for it to go to a small select committee which would be able to hear all arguments and make a decision that would not be

completely a government decision but one that would take into consideration the views of the various associations and unions representing civil servants and the views of those who are not now immediately within the scope of the civil service.
There will be an opportunity for these organizations to appear and I am quite sure that this will result in a better act which will not only benefit the operations of the government but will make civil servants themselves feel that they have a greater say in their affairs and an enhanced opportunity for advancement with the result that they will have an increased desire to remain within the sphere of the civil service.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I should like to refer to the brief submitted to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) by the conseil de la vie franpaise with regard to the ratio of bilingual or French-speaking Canadians in the federal civil service. Since 90 per cent of bilingual civil servants are French Canadians and since, at the same time, the number of French Canadians in the civil service is only half of what it should be, it follows that in large sections of the public administration bilingualism is non-existent to such an extent that the language of communication within the departments is the English language and that the French Canadian taxpayer is often hard put to be served in his own language.
In our humble opinion, an even more serious result stems from the influence of the civil service over the administration of Canada and the very life of the nation. Because the majority of civil servants have no knowledge whatsoever of one of the official languages and cultures in our country, the French speaking citizens are ruled according to standards of thought which are exclusively English. It is no surprise, therefore, that they are increasingly being excluded from the federal administration, the public services, the armed forces and the large crown corporations. In short, they are being deprived of the place to which they are entitled in their own country.
Drastic reforms are necessary if Canada is to remain a bilingual and bicultural country, a country where Canadians of French origin will feel at home. Such reforms have been suggested on various occasions. We shall not go over them today. In the circumstances, one can readily understand that the French Canadians are hardly attracted to the federal service, in view of the fact that entry requirements are based exclusively on English standards and that they must give up their language in the actual performance of their duties.
Mr. Speaker, let me quote another excerpt of this brief:
Nine departments have shown an increase of 2.3 per cent in the number of French Canadians, as compared to the total number of employees between

those departments: veterans affairs, agriculture, the Auditor General, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, fisheries, national revenue, secretary of state, labour, national film board.
On the other hand, the proportion of French-Canadian employees has dropped in 15 departments.

trade and commerce, civil service commission, national research council, national defence, finance, printing bureau, justice, mines and technical surveys, post office, resources and economic development, national health and welfare, transport and public works. I wanted to make those few remarks, and I should like to add this. I would be remiss in failing to point out that apartheid is not confined to South Africa; it is also found in the civil service generally. It may come as a surprise to some hon. members that in certain departments it is considered wrong to speak French; French-Canadian civil servants have to use the English language among themselves. That should not be.

Civil Service Act
It would therefore be well to investigate the matter with a view to exposing the situation and seeing that justice is done.
Indeed, I feel it is unthinkable that such a situation should be allowed to exist. If I am correctly informed-and I made a serious inquiry in the matter-I ask that the situation be looked into so that an end may be put to what I consider to be discrimination against one of the two official languages of this country.
Mr. Speaker, I think this bill concerning the civil service is not only timely, but overdue. The act has not been amended for the last 40 years. It was time that this government did something about it because there are very few acts in our statutes that have not been amended for the last 40 years.
This was not our job, Mr. Speaker, but since our predecessors have been neglectful on that point, this government has to take action.
I am not telling anything new when I say that all is not to the best in the federal	civil
service. Every	year, many	of our	best	civilservants leave	the federal	service	and	takeup other jobs.	This is not	normal.	Nor	is it
normal to let them go without doing anything to keep them, unless we want to maintain some sections of our public service as sanctuaries for complacent mediocrities.
However, in considering this very important bill, I believe the time has come to smash certain idols in the civil service, to cut down to size some of the demigods of high officialdom who think they can do anything because of their permanent status, and finally to reveal some of the scheming that cripples efficient administration and puts the whole civil service to shame.
Mr. Speaker, efforts are made to attract able people into the civil service. Why not first try to keep those who are already in the service, instead of treating like outcasts people who have proved their ability in related fields and who are scoffed at, ridiculed and deceived in the civil service, often by backward and incompetent officials.
I am not usually violent, but my association, two years ago, with the standing committee on estimates, enabled me to get acquainted with certain problems of federal administration. I took that opportunity to investigate matters and question people, and what we learned was not too nice. However, that unrewarding and disappointing work gained me

the confidence of many civil servants who, in the hope of getting some improvement, took me into their confidence.
I received many letters and telephone calls, and many visitors. Some of those civil servants were acting from fear because they were afraid of reprisals in case it should be known that they had discussed their problems with a member of parliament. And I know that some section heads-not the more clever ones-will say: What does that member know about the civil service? What right has he to stick his nose into our business? To those people let me say in the first place that I was a civil servant myself for several years, during which I met, like anywhere else, men who were worthy of confidence, but also some very poor officials who were unworthy of the government's confidence. Let me also say that as an elected representative of the Canadian people, I have a right to know what goes on in the civil service and that it is even my responsibility to make sure that the government uses the people and the funds voted by parliament to give this country the first class service it deserves.
If the civil servants are not treated fairly by their superiors, they do right to talk things over with their representatives. It is our business to preside over the public welfare and to redress grievances. And I have known enough distressing cases to assure you that the need is there.
I have therefore been informed of many cases of injustice and maladministration brought to my attention by civil servants. Some of them were perhaps inclined to exaggerate, but most of them had a healthy attitude but were driven to desperation by the lack of understanding, indeed the incompetence of their superiors. I am under the impression that while our civil service includes an overwhelming majority of very good employees it also includes a distressing minority of political creatures who are an obstacle to efficient public administration and who tend to create a general atmosphere of fear and oppression. That must be stopped. An act of parliament, whatever its merits, will be of no avail unless we can change the morale of the civil service, unless we get rid of the deadwood, steeped in inefficiency and favouritism.
We have some very good civil servants, but there is a long way between that and blissfully accepting the hackneyed claim that it is the "best civil service in the world". That I cannot believe in view of the things I have been told in confidence.

I am quite prepared to admit, Mr. Speaker, that those may have been special cases. That was my own reaction at first. But today, I am convinced that there is in the public service a clique whose leaders are found among the political creatures who never could stomach the defeats of 1957 and 1958. I will not mention names at this time, but my colleagues know as well as I do about the wall that stands in our way whenever we try to get information or find out the reasons for a particular appointment or promotion. There are people there who protect themselves, people who care little about the efficient administration of public affairs but are more concerned with trying to work against the government, so that the people will turn against it at the next elections. I know, Mr. Speaker, that this is a serious charge, and I say it with severity, because we in this house are faced with a government within the government. When you have to ask two or three different questions to elicit information from witnesses appearing before committees, when witnesses plead ignorance of the facts or refuse to disclose some information, it looks bad. In my opinion, a reform is necessary.
No private industry could survive if it were administered as the government is in some departments. No businessman could keep from boiling over if he saw the favouritism and incompetence which prevail in some areas of the administration-and I am not referring to the fact that some civil servants hardly get 40 minutes off for lunch. Not one of us in this house would accept to work under conditions such as are the lot of some civil servants. How could we allow such a situation to endure and civil servants to be subjected to it without even having the right to complain?
Perhaps you would like some proof of my assertions; perhaps you want to know what the civil servants are silently complaining about, because they do not dare raise their voices lest they be ostracized or punished or cast aside. I could read many letters I have received; I could draw a long list of their grievances; and all this would be only the voice of those who have had the courage to protest a situation that this government has inherited from its predecessors who appointed to some key positions their minions and their sbirros.
Do you want to know what the complaints are about? They are about daily inequities; they are about maladministration in some departments; they are about the inefficiency and partisan spirit of some officials. And I limit myself strictly to the charges I felt
Civil Service Act
bound to make because they concern the administration of public affairs.
I will spare you the petty or scurvy tricks and private spite which can develop into every day fare, and can be exercised particularly two or three times a year when the head of a branch prepares an efficiency rating concerning each of the employees under him.
That is the time when promotions are settled for those who knuckle down and hold their tongue, for those who work like slaves so that their supervisor may go to a higher official and brag smugly about the high efficiency of his department; but it is also the time when some are eliminated because they are not found fit for the job, but suited, not always on professional grounds.
If an underling dares offer a suggestion or make a protest against an injustice, it will be entered on his rating, unknown to him, that he is refractory and steps towards his dismissal will even be taken should a difficult situation develop. Afterwards any legal procedure before the courts will be carefully avoided if the civil servant who feels he has been wronged wants to appeal to the courts and to assert his rights as a free citizen.
This method of evaluating the conduct and efficiency of their staff can turn to be the most sinister weapons in the hands of devious supervisors. There are also complaints about the narrow-mindedness of some officials viciously persecuting employees who are only trying to do their duty on religious holidays- which they should do-and who grin and ridicule people who want to comply with the requirements of their faith.
Others claim that some officials tried to stop their subordinates from voting in the province of Quebec, claiming that the government of the day was led by a man with whom the federal Prime Minister was not on good terms. I hardly need to quote any names.
Moreover, there are protests against officials who tolerate a whole section considering itself above all rules and regulations, and who allow their favourites to arrive at the office at any odd time in the morning, whereas other civil servants have to take a cut in salary when they come late because of a storm or because they missed their transfer to another bus, or again, because of some stupid closing of the bridge to Hull. Neither do I need to quote any names here, for here again, those responsible for this discrimination will recognize themselves.
There are grievances against high officials who are never there when some decision must

Civil Service Act
be taken or who make their subordinates work after regular hours out of sheer maladministration.
Others again claim-and this is almost unjust and even insolent-that all civil servants are not entitled to the same number of holidays and that leave is not in proportion to the working days. People complain that overtime, or additional time periods, are in most cases not paid in cash but that employees have to work three and a half hours on end to earn half a day's leave, which in many cases they would rather not have, in order not to be compelled to add those three and a half hours to their normal day of work. And again, overtime has to be calculated as from the moment when the employee signs in which means, if it is Saturday morning, that he may have to spend an hour in the bus coming to the office and another hour when he goes back home.
Some also claim that in the odd branch and the odd department, employees are prevented from taking their holidays when they please. There are some seasons when public servants may not be absent, and they live outside normal society. They are told that no one asked them to work and that they can go and find employment elsewhere. Is that a way of dealing with public servants? Would you and I accept to be treated in this way? After all, those people are our employees, and it is up to us to teach a lesson to some officials who are unfair to the minor civil servants.
Some claim, moreover, that civil servants cannot air their grievances, because the associations which represent them, though they are doing their best, do not have the authority of a professional organization.
These complaints had to do with ascertained and repeated inequities. I might also point out certain grievances no less serious but more difficult to eliminate, cases of obvious mismanagement. Civil servants wrote to me and came to see me to say that they are losing faith in civil service commission examinations because of the results and promotions. That is serious, and if you refer to some of the answers given last year in the committee of the house during the discussion of the operation of the civil service commission, you will find that the witnesses were unable to swear that all the positions under the commission had always been and are still being filled on the basis of competence. This is another thing we inherited from our predecessors.

How is it that applicants for the same examination, who all know each other, who know each other's ability and qualifications after working together for years often find that the less qualified candidates succeed, get promotions and are sent abroad.
How is it that it is often known beforehand that such or such an applicant, for reasons known to their competitors, will certainly be the only ones who qualify? And if unsuccessful candidates make enquiries, they are told to write to the secretary of the commission or to ask for a review of their examination sheets. And of course, when those sheets are reviewed, it is found that the examining officers have not marked them, that it is just a simple appreciation given by anonymous examiners and that it is a a foregone conclusion that the review will confirm the results of the original examination. It is a serious situation, Mr. Speaker, and I have received enough complaints to believe that such doings which are beyond even the commission's control, are the responsibility of a clique of examiners who form a kind of family compact and regard their jobs as a game preserve.
May I continue, Mr. Speaker? It is six o'clock.
